However, AC-4, AC-5, and AC-6 explicitly demand asserting new matching logic for those exact inputs. Adding these assertions to the grandfathered file (capped at 317 lines) will trip the bloat baseline hook immediately.
findings.suggestion: Re-add the `test_classify_complexity.py` baseline bump back into IT-0. You cannot satisfy the ACs without adding test code, and splitting these specific tests into a fragmented secondary test file just to dodge a baseline hook is anti-pattern.

findings.finding: Cross-platform configuration drift. The plan targets `fnmatch` for matching `TOUCHES_BUILD_BASENAME_GLOBS` and mandates Windows separator support in AC-4. Standard Python `fnmatch.fnmatch()` evaluates based on the host

The central safety argument for capping history-derived complexity at `small` depends on Stage 2 recovering genuinely broader changes. However, the proposed recovery is a mandatory instruction in `references/iteration-planning.md`, not an enforced classification path. A skipped, incomplete, or incorrectly executed Quick Scout would now allow a cross-component change to remain `small`, bypassing integration/cross-layer checks, the review floor, and spec/plan gates that the prior incidentally triggered.
findings.suggestion: Make the diff-driven detector results an enforceable input to final complexity selection, not solely a Scout checklist item. Persist the file list and detector results in the run record, require Stage 2 to record them before complexity is locked, and fail or retain the conservative tier when required detector evidence is absent. Add end-to-end tests proving that a no-keyword change touching multiple components, CI/supply-chain files, IO boundaries, and Python build inputs reaches the intended floor and activates the corresponding phases.

findings.finding: fnmatch` over an `os.path.basename()` result will not satisfy AC-4’s Windows-separator requirement when tests run on Linux/macOS: `os.path.basename("dir\\uv.lock")` treats the backslash as an ordinary character. Consequently, the proposed glob mechanism can miss Windows-style paths despite appearing correct for normal repository paths.
findings.suggestion: Normalize detector inputs to repository-style POSIX paths before basename extraction, or explicitly use `PureWindowsPath`/separator normalization for detection. Add tests for nested `\`-separated paths for every literal and globbed Python build input, plus mixed-separator paths if those can enter the detector.

findings.finding: The proposed message regex, `requirements[\w.-]\.txt`, is not bounded. Depending on the existing matching API, it can match `my-requirements.txt`, `requirements.txt.bak`, or a filename embedded in a longer token—while the diff detector explicitly promises not to match these partial-basename cases. The plan’s prose-only guard does not address filename partial matches on the message surface.
findings.suggestion: Define message matching semantics explicitly and use filename/token boundaries appropriate to the current regex engine, for example boundaries that reject preceding/following filename characters (`[\w.-]`). Escape literal-dot filenames such as `pyproject.toml` and `setup.py`, and add negative message tests paralleling AC-5, not merely the “requirements catalog” prose case.

findings.finding: Recording `prior_source` in F5c changes the persisted iterate-entry shape. Although the writer accepts arbitrary `--entry-json` fields, the plan does not establish whether readers, schemas, snapshots, export tools, or cross-repository consumers validate or normalize those entries. A permissive writer does not prove compatibility with all readers.
findings.suggestion: Audit the schema/validation and all history readers before adding the field. Define `prior_source` as a stable enum with backward-compatible handling for historical entries that lack it, and add a round-trip test through the real F5c writer and history loader. Ensure unknown/missing values cannot accidentally be interpreted as a history-qualified entry when the deferred “keyword-only history” calibration is later implemented.

findings.finding: AC-3 relies on “this repo’s real store,” whose rolling last-20/last-50 contents naturally change as iterates run. A test directly against that store will become time-dependent and may fail or silently stop testing the stated scenario after routine activity changes the median.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the measured real-store probe as evidence, but implement automated tests using fixed history fixtures representing cold start, trivial-dominated, medium-dominated, and all-large histories. Test the production store only as an optional diagnostic/integration probe with an asserted observation recorded for this run, not as the deterministic regression test.

findings.finding: The proposed documentation drift protection is incomplete for the actual detector model. `TOUCHES_BUILD_FILE_PATTERNS` intentionally excludes `requirements.txt`, while `TOUCHES_BUILD_BASENAME_GLOBS` and `RISK_TAXONOMY` supply part of the effective trigger set. A bidirectional drift test against only `TOUCHES_BUILD_FILE_PATTERNS` can pass while docs omit globbed files or message detection diverges from diff detection.
findings.suggestion: Define one canonical effective Python build-input set for documentation/testing—derived from literals plus globs—and test all three representations: diff detector, message taxonomy, and the SKILL/docs trigger rows. Keeping the separate literal tuple and glob tuple is reasonable because of their different matching semantics; duplicating the actual input inventory across unrelated tests and docs is not.

findings.finding: The consolidation explicitly warns that IT-5 changes which phases fire and must occur clearly before or after REQ-3, not during it. This mini-plan states that it is a lever for following iterates but does not explicitly declare its execution/merge boundary relative to REQ-3 or any already-running campaign work. The behavioral change can alter required gates and evidence expectations for work already in progress.
findings.suggestion: Make the scheduling decision a precondition of the iterate: either merge IT-5 before REQ-3 begins, or defer it until REQ-3 completes. Do not apply the new classifier to an already-created run/config without an explicit migration decision and recorded rationale.

findings.finding: The stale-baseline correction is useful, but “this run does not touch `test_classify_complexity.py`” is not a sufficient bloat preflight for this change. New classifier behavior, history metadata, and path matching need regression coverage somewhere, and any edited or newly added oversized test/support file can independently trigger the stop-hook.
findings.suggestion: Before implementation, enumerate the actual planned changed files—including test fixtures and documentation drift tests—and run the bloat/ratchet preflight over that complete set. Update the anchor/evidence record to reflect that IT-5 is no longer blocked by the formerly missing baseline, avoiding stale sequencing assumptions for later orchestration.

findings.finding: There is no new authentication, untrusted-input execution, or data-exposure surface in the proposed changes. The practical security-adjacent concern is reduced assurance: misclassification to `small` can suppress review and coverage gates for changes to sensitive workflow, dependency, or IO files.
findings.suggestion: Treat the enforced diff-driven floor in finding 1 as a security/assurance control as well as a calibration feature, and include workflow/dependency-file scenarios in the end-to-end phase-selection tests.  Overall, the diagnosis and the Python build-input split are sound, and the plan correctly avoids broadening into unmeasured ecosystems. It needs an enforceable—not documentation-only—Stage-2 recovery path plus path/regex and persisted-schema safeguards before the reduction in default process can be safely shipped. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
